doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Depression-era Kirkland and everybody making music
summary: Crow explains that becoming a professional musician was unimaginable then, and that community singing and school bands fed the Swing Era's big-band togetherness.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Did this influence your eventually coming to New York?

Well when I came to New York it was on the suggestion — you know I’d been in the Army for a while and I had been out here on a visit once just out of high school. But the idea of ever leaving Kirkland, Washington was not a strong possibility. You know we were depression kids and just the idea that anybody would go anywhere else in the first place you didn’t think you could afford it. You might go to Seattle, but that’s about the limit of our scope at that time. And the idea that anybody would become a professional musician was not within our realm of possibility because we didn’t know any. We knew some music teachers. And we knew lots of amateur musicians. Everybody was a musician in those days.

Well you know in the 20s and 30s, everybody at least sang. I remember singing almost everywhere I went. If we went to church we sang. If we went to an American Legion meeting we sang. If we went to somebody’s house within a half hour after dinner we would be around the piano singing the songs everybody knew. You know, Stephen Foster songs, World War I songs, stuff like that. And everybody sang. There was no such thing as somebody without a voice. There were people that it was understood they didn’t have strong voices, or that they sang a little sharp or that the quality of their voice was a little raspy, but that didn’t make pariahs of them. Everybody was expected to try and the strong singers carried it. So we’ve come to an age now where we lean on professionals tremendously. We’ve become watchers instead of participants. And I think it’s kind of unfortunate because there was a quality of sharing that music experience in the community singing and the school bands and that whole thing that was I think the Swing Era, that kind of playing that went on in big bands, was a direct outgrowth of that. It was the whole thrill of playing well together in a big band is becoming really skilled at getting

together like that. Everybody appreciated barber shop harmony and that sort of thing, and when you got into a big band and could play riffs together or could read dumb stock together and really make it into some music, that was a thrilling achievement.
